title: switch
summary: `switch` compares **one** value against a list of fixed options and jumps to the matching `case`. End each case with `break`, or execution carries on into the next one.
markdown:
## One value, many options

A long `if` / `else if` chain that keeps testing the same variable against fixed values is clearer as a `switch`.

```cpp
#include <iostream>

int main()
{
    int choice{};
    std::cin >> choice;

    switch (choice)
    {
    case 1:
        std::cout << "Starting a new game\n";
        break;
    case 2:
        std::cout << "Loading\n";
        break;
    case 3:
        std::cout << "Goodbye\n";
        break;
    default:
        std::cout << "Not an option\n";
        break;
    }
    return 0;
}
```

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    X{"switch (choice)"} -->|"case 1"| A["New game"]
    X -->|"case 2"| B["Load"]
    X -->|"case 3"| C["Quit"]
    X -->|"default"| D["Not an option"]
```

| Part | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `switch (value)` | The value to examine |
| `case 1:` | Where to jump to when the value is 1 |
| `break;` | Leave the `switch` |
| `default:` | Where to jump to when no case matches |

## Fall-through

A `case` is only a **label**: a place to jump to. It is not a block with an end. Without `break`, execution simply continues into whatever comes next.

```
 switch (2)
 case 1:   print "one"
 case 2:   print "two"      jumps in here
 case 3:   print "three"    no break above, so this runs too
 default:  print "other"    and so does this

 Output: two three other
```

Forgetting a `break` is the classic `switch` bug.

Fall-through is useful in one situation: several values that share the same code.

```cpp
switch (letter)
{
case 'a':
case 'e':
case 'i':
case 'o':
case 'u':
    std::cout << "vowel\n";
    break;
default:
    std::cout << "consonant\n";
    break;
}
```

> [!tip] Marking it as deliberate
> If a case does some work and you **want** it to continue into the next, write `[[fallthrough]];` at that point. It tells the compiler and the reader that the missing `break` is intended.

## `return` also leaves

Inside a function, a `return` ends the function, and therefore the `switch`. No `break` is needed after it.

```cpp
std::string_view dayName(int day)
{
    switch (day)
    {
    case 1: return "Monday";
    case 2: return "Tuesday";
    case 3: return "Wednesday";
    default: return "unknown";
    }
}
```

## The rules

| Rule | Detail |
|---|---|
| The value must be integer-like | `int`, `char`, `bool` or an enum. Not `std::string`, not `double`. |
| Each `case` must be a constant | A literal, or a `constexpr` value. Not an ordinary variable. |
| No ranges | There is no `case 1 to 5`. Use `if` for ranges. |
| Variables inside a case need braces | `case 1: { int x{ 5 }; ... break; }` |

## `switch` or `if`?

| Use `switch` when | Use `if` when |
|---|---|
| Comparing **one** value against several fixed values | Testing ranges, such as `score >= 90` |
| Menus, commands, single characters, enums | Text, decimals or conditions that combine several variables |

`switch` becomes much more valuable once you meet enums in [[4.05 Enums]], where the compiler can warn you if you forget one of the options.

## Check yourself
```quiz
? Can you `switch` on a `std::string`?
- Yes, like any other type
+ No, only integer-like types such as `int`, `char`, `bool` and enums
- Yes, but only if every `case` is a string literal
- Only for strings of one character
> `switch` needs an integer-like value. To choose on text, use an `if` / `else if` chain.

? What happens when a case has no `break`?
- The compiler reports an error
- The `switch` ends anyway after that case
+ Execution continues into the next case's statements
- The program jumps to `default`
> This is fall-through: without `break` (or `return`), execution runs straight on into the next case.

? What is `default` for?
+ It is where execution goes when the value matches none of the cases
- It is the case that always runs first
- It sets the value being switched on when it is missing
- It is required, or the `switch` will not compile
> `default` catches every value with no matching `case`. It is optional, but a good place to handle unexpected values.

? When is fall-through the right thing?
- When every case should run all the cases below it
- When you forgot which case should run
+ When several values should share the same code
> Stacking `case 'a': case 'e': ...` above one block makes them share code. Elsewhere, fall-through is usually a missing `break`.
```
ideas:
1. Read a number from 1 to 7 and print the name of the day.
2. Build a small calculator: read `a op b`, where `op` is a `char`, and `switch` on `op`.
3. Remove one `break` on purpose and watch the fall-through.
